Action.description: What will happen to one entry.

oneOf.description: Comment it out and say so, because it has been edited since omt wrote it.

unmapped.description:
Methods the adapter had no mapping for, verbatim.

Reported rather than dropped, because a protocol source that silently
ignores what it does not understand degrades into a worse one while
still claiming its tier — and this is the list that says which.

accept.description: Explicit confirmation. Nothing happens without it.

plan.description: The hash of the plan being accepted.

preserved.description: How many were commented out because they had been edited.

steps.description: What was done, step by step.

error.description: Why it failed, when it did.

files_changed.description:
How many files it changed, once it has finished.

The first thing anybody comparing two attempts looks at, and the reason
it is here rather than left to a client to compute from a diff.

workspace.description: The workspace its worktree opens as.

location.description: Where it lives, relative to the state directory.

mode.description: The permission bits it must have.

sensitive.description: Whether it can hold something somebody would not want copied.

path.description: The absolute path the blob was materialised at.

baseline_working_secs.description: The usual working time for this binding.

consecutive_failures.description: How many results in a row have failed.

since_file_change_secs.description: How long since a file last changed.

tokens_since_file_change.description: Tokens spent since a file last changed.

working_secs.description: How long it has been working, in seconds.

detail.description: A line somebody can act on.

reasons.description: Every reason, never just the first.

limit.description: Most entries to return, newest last.

dropped.description:
How many fell off the front of a bounded log, so a partial one is never
presented as whole.

entries.description: Oldest first, so a reader follows what happened in order.

conflicts.description: Everything omt's own defaults would take, worst first.

programs_known.description:
How many programs the registry knows about.

Reported so an empty result can be told apart from a registry that
knows nothing — "no conflicts" from a check that examined nothing looks
exactly like "no conflicts" from one that examined everything.

intent.description:
The intent id, where the call carried one — which is what lets a repeat
be recognised as the same intent rather than counted as a second.

auth_backend.description: Whether a password or bearer token is configured.

binds.description: Where omt would listen: `unix`, `loopback`, `tailnet`, or an address.

default_role.description: What an unauthenticated caller gets: `none`, `viewer` or `operator`.

trust_proxy.description: Whether a reverse proxy is declared to terminate it.

refusals.description: Everything that must be fixed, not just the first.

warnings.description: Things worth knowing that do not stop it.

BindingProblemOut.description: Something wrong with a keybinding file.

from.description: Skip this many lines from the start, for paging through a long one.

lines.description:
Most lines to return.

A block can hold a whole test run, and a phone that asks for one over a
slow link is a phone that stalls. The default is what fits a screen and
a scroll; a caller that wants everything asks for it.

command.description: The command that produced it, where the shell marked one.

lines.description:
The output, as styled runs — the same encoding the screen uses, so a
client has one renderer rather than two.

total.description: How many lines the block holds in total.

truncated.description: Whether more remain after what was returned.

BlockSummary.description: One command and what came of it.

attributed.description:
Whether omt ever saw the command this block belongs to.

False for a block opened from output alone — a shell with no OSC 133, a
bare `ssh`, a container. A surface must not offer "re-run" for one of
these: there is no command, and the alternative is scraping the screen
for something that looks like a prompt.

command.description: The command as the shell marked it.

exit_code.description: The exit code, where the shell reported one.

failed.description: Whether a surface should show this as a failure.

id.description: Its id, which is what a client refers to when it asks to re-run one.

outcome.description:
`running`, `exited`, or `unknown` — the last meaning the shell said the
command ended and did not say how, which is not the same as success.

output_row.description: Where its output starts, counting from the first line ever written.

CandidateIn.description: One candidate, as the caller describes it.

exit.description: The exit code, where there was one.

in_scope.description: Whether it is in the workspace the search came from.

session_active.description: Whether its session is still running.

session.description: Which session's screen to write down.

lines.description: Most lines to return, counting back from the end.

agent.description: The agent omt believes is there, where it believes anything.

regions.description:
What each named region of it contains.

The screen alone is what somebody already has. What they cannot see is
where `after_last_rule` starts, which is the single thing that decides
whether their rule fires on the question or on the scrollback above it.

total.description:
How many lines the session has in total.

So a script can tell a complete capture from a truncated one, which a
line count alone cannot.

CapturedRegion.description: One region, and what is in it.

name.description: Its name, as a rule would write it.

effects.description: What omt does when it runs.

origin.description:
Which tier it belongs to.

Declared rather than hidden, per 03 §3.6: a core capability was checked
by the macro and appears in every generated artifact; a plugin's
registers at run time and can appear in none of them. A client that
could not tell them apart would have no way to explain why one of them
is missing from its generated union.

CatalogHash.description:
What identifies a catalog.

A client caches the catalog and sends the hash it has; a matching hash
means "nothing to send". It must therefore cover **everything a client
would render differently** — which is why it is computed from the entries
rather than from the binary's version: two builds with the same version and
a different plugin enabled are different catalogs, and a client that
believed otherwise would render a stale list of what it can do.

known_hash.description:
The hash the caller already has.

A matching hash means "nothing to send", which is the point of the
catalog being cacheable at all: a phone reconnecting on a train should
not pull two hundred schemas to learn that none of them changed
([03 §3.5.1](../../../docs/architecture/03-capability-catalog.md)).

entries.description: Every capability, in name order. Omitted when `unchanged`.

unchanged.description:
Whether the caller's cached copy is still current.

When true, `entries` is empty because there was nothing to say — not
because there are no capabilities. Two different facts, and a client
that conflated them would render an empty instance.

Check.description: One thing that was looked at.

detail.description: What was found, in words somebody can act on.

remedy.description: What to do about it. Present whenever the verdict is not `ok`.

mouse_reporting.description: Whether the program in the pane has enabled mouse reporting.

consumed.description: Whether omt took it, or the program under it did.

term.description:
The terminal the human is actually sitting in front of.

Supplied by the caller because only the client knows it. Keyed off
`TERM` rather than `$TMUX`, which does not survive ssh — getting that
backwards yields a copy that works locally and silently does nothing
remotely.

text.description: The text to put on the local clipboard.

message.description:
What the surface may say about it.

Not "copied". OSC 52 has no acknowledgement, Terminal.app does not
implement it at all, and kitty refuses silently above its own limit.

sequence.description: The bytes to write into the session's output stream.

runs.description: The runs to put side by side.

caveats.description: What is not comparable, and why.

rows.description: One row per run, in the order given.

key.description: A dotted key, or absent for everything.

unmapped.description:
What it did not, by name, with why.

Reported rather than dropped: an import that silently ignores half a
config leaves somebody wondering why their font is wrong, and looking in
the wrong place for the answer.

usual_paths.description:
Where this tool usually keeps its settings, so a client can offer to
read one rather than asking somebody to find it.

values.description: What omt understood, as dotted keys.

ConfigValue.description: One resolved setting and where it came from.

file.description: The file it came from, where there was one.

ConflictOut.description: One thing a binding would break.

does.description: What the key does there, in that program's own words.

verified_against.description: What that keymap was checked against, so a stale warning is visible.

chord.description: The canonical form of the chord that was asked about.

conflicts.description: Everything it would break, worst first.

refused.description: Whether omt refuses to take it by default.

client.description: What the client called itself in the handshake.

id.description: Its connection id, unique for as long as it is connected.

agents.description:
Every agent omt knows how to drive, found or not.

All of them, not only the ones present: somebody whose agent is missing
needs to see that omt knows about it and did not find it, which is a
different problem from omt never having heard of it.

searched.description:
Whether `PATH` was readable at all.

Distinguished from finding nothing, because an unreadable `PATH` makes
every answer below meaningless and saying "no agents" would be a
confident wrong answer.

devices.description:
Newest first, because the one somebody is about to revoke is usually the
one they just noticed.

revoked.description:
Whether this call is what revoked it.

False for one already revoked, which is not an error: a second tap on a
row somebody already dealt with should not look like a failure.

DeviceSummary.description: One device that has been let in.

bound.description:
Whether the credential is bound to a key the device holds.

False for a browser, and honestly so: a key in local storage is
exfiltrated with the token it would protect, so binding there is theatre.

id.description: The credential's id, which is what revoking names.

label.description: What the device called itself when it joined.

from.description: Where it was, for a rename.

Directive.description: One line of a tmux config, and what omt makes of it.

capability.description: The omt capability it becomes, where there is one.

line.description: Which line it was, so somebody can find it.

mapping.description: What omt can do with it.

note.description: Why, in words somebody can act on.

Disagreement.description: Something the advertised `TERM` and the terminal in use disagree about.

observed.description: What the terminal appears to actually be.

trigger.description: A trigger the user just produced, if this call is reporting one.

recorded.description: Whether the reported trigger was recognised.

surface.description: The one feature omt has earned the right to mention, if any.

hint.description: One hint by id, or nothing to turn them all off.

silenced.description: Whether the lot were turned off.

group.description: One group, or every group when absent.

checks.description: Every check, in the order they were run.

failures.description: How many came out badly, so a caller can lead with the number.

not_checked.description: How many were not run at all.

expected_version.description: The version it is expected to be at.

binding.description: Which binding. Not the session: a session id alone is not a target.

valid_for_seconds.description: Seconds after which the entry is re-confirmed rather than sent.

state.description:
Where it has got to, which on a mirrored queue is `pending` until the
agent writes its receipt.

Entry.description: One thing that happened, as a client renders it.

synthetic.description:
Whether omt sent it on somebody's behalf rather than a human typing
it — a synthetic turn must never be shown as a human one.

oneOf.description:
The agent's own reasoning, kept apart from what it said.

Separate because it is a different kind of claim and a client should be
able to collapse it: reasoning rendered as speech reads as the agent
telling you things it has not decided.

output.description: What it produced, where it produced anything.

oneOf.description: The agent's plan, as it now stands.

steps.description: The steps, re-rendered in place on each revision.

oneOf.description:
Something omt does not model, reported by its own name rather than
dropped.

category.description: The agent's own category for it.

EventKind.description:
Which family an event belongs to.

Closed, so a client can filter a subscription by kind and know it is not
silently missing a family nobody told it about. An event with no kind would
be unsubscribable, which is why every payload has one.

oneOf.description: Terminal output, blocks and grid changes.
Who is attached and what they are doing.

rule.description: The rule that decided, where one did.

summary.description: In words, for somebody looking at a wrong answer.

action.description: What omt does with it, if anything.

alias.description: The alias installed beside it, where there is one.

awkward.description: Whether it needs an AltGr on a common non-US layout.

conflicts.description: What it would take from the program underneath.

in_a_pane.description:
What happens in a pane that is passing through.

Said plainly, because "not bound" and "bound but the pane owns it" look
identical from a user's chair and have different fixes.

branch.description: The branch that won, which is what to merge.

merged.description:
What omt did *not* do, said plainly.

Choosing records the choice. Merging is a decision with conflicts in it,
and a tool that merges when you tap "choose" is one you stop trusting
the first time it picks wrong.

agents.description: The agents to run, by the names the catalog uses.

base.description: The revision every worktree branches from. Absent means the current one.

name.description:
What to call this fan-out, so it can be asked about later — from another
client, on another device.

prompt.description: The prompt every arm is given.

workspace.description: Which workspace's repository the worktrees come from.

arms.description:
Every arm, including the ones that failed to start.

Every one, not only the failures: a fan-out that half-started and said
"error" leaves somebody to work out which of four agents is missing.

name.description: Which fan-out. Absent lists them all.

chosen.description: The agent whose arm was chosen, when one has been.

complete.description: Whether every arm has finished or failed.

kinds.description: Only these kinds. Empty means all.

sessions.description: Only these sessions. Empty means all.

governs.description:
Which modes a modal keymap is allowed to touch at all.

Reported because it is the rule that makes the feature safe, and a rule
nobody can read is one nobody can check.

FoundAgent.description: One agent, and whether it is here.

path.description: Where it is, if it is anywhere.

is_symlink.description: Whether it is a symlink — reported, not followed silently.

rel.description: Its workspace-relative path, which a client sends back.

path.description: A workspace-relative path. Empty means the root.

chunks.description: How many there are, so a client can show a bar rather than a spinner.

media_type.description:
What it appears to be, sniffed from the bytes rather than the name — an
extension is a claim and the content is the fact.

chunks.description: How many there are in total.

complete.description: Whether the file is now complete and on disk.

remaining.description: How many are still missing, which is what a progress bar is drawn from.

size.description: How many bytes they decode to.

staged.description: Whether to take the staged diff rather than the unstaged one.

base.description: Compare against this revision instead of the index.

branch.description: The branch, or absent on a detached head.

untracked.description: Files git does not know about.

HelpEntry.description: One entry of a rendered help page.

role.description: What it needs to be allowed to do.

HintOut.description: The hint to show, if there is one.

next.description: The single hint to offer, or nothing.

remaining.description: How many are left, so a client can say "3 more tips" honestly.

runs.description: How many times omt has run.

every_run.description: Show every run rather than one row per command.

of.description: What the scope names, where it names something.

held.description:
How many are held in total, so an empty result can be told apart from
an empty history.

exit_code.description: How it ended, where that was seen.

lines.description:
The lines themselves, each prefixed as git prefixes them.

Prefixed rather than split into added and removed: the order is what
makes a diff readable, and two lists lose it.

new_start.description: Where it starts in the new file.

old_lines.description: How many lines it covers there.

old_start.description: Where it starts in the old file.

IdentityDevice.description: One device, under the person who holds it.

bound.description:
Whether a key it holds backs the credential.

False for a browser, and recorded as false rather than papered over: a
key in local storage is exfiltrated with the token it would protect, so
binding there would be a claim omt cannot keep.

identities.description: Everybody this instance knows, with their devices.

devices.description: How many devices this took away.

IdentitySummary.description: One person, and the devices they hold.

agent.description: Which agent to install it for.
Which agent it is being considered for.

rules.description:
The rule set, as text.

Text rather than a path, so the caller decides where it came from and
omt never reads a file it was not handed.
What each rule concludes and where it looks, in the order they decide.

shipped.description: How many rules the shipped set has, for comparison.

InspectedRule.description: One rule, as a person reads it.

priority.description: Which rule wins when two match.

option.description:
The chosen option, by the agent's own label — verbatim, so the recorded
answer can be compared against what was sent when confirming delivery.

text.description: Free text, where the question allowed it.

state.description:
Its state after the answer.

`resolving`, not `confirmed`: omt has claimed the right to answer and
nothing more. For a synthetic responder the far side is a UI omt does
not own, and confirmation comes from observing it, never from the write
succeeding.

InteractionSummary.description: One card, as a remote surface needs it.

deliverable.description:
Whether omt can deliver an answer, and over what.

A surface renders its buttons from this and never from the state: a card
that is open but has no channel must not offer a button, or the user
finds out by the wrong option being selected.

id.description: Its id, which is how it is answered.

kind.description: What kind of card it is.

not_deliverable_because.description: Why not, when it cannot be answered here.

options.description: The options, verbatim and in the agent's own order.

prompt.description: The question or the command, rendered for a small screen.

state.description: Where it is in its lifecycle.

expires_in_secs.description: How many seconds it remains exchangeable.

invite.description: The invite, shown once. Exchanged for a credential by whoever scans it.

daily_at_secs.description: Or fire daily, this many seconds past midnight.

every_seconds.description: Fire every this many seconds. Zero or absent means manual.

name.description:
What to call it. Also its identity: creating one with a name already in
use replaces it, which is what makes editing a job possible without a
separate update call.

workspace.description:
The workspace it runs in, by id.

An id, like every other capability that names a workspace. It took a
directory path, which meant the generated client — whose parameter is
called `workspace` everywhere and carries an id everywhere else — got
`is not a directory` for the one obvious call.

replaced.description: Whether an existing job of the same name was replaced.

consecutive_failures.description:
How many times it has failed in a row.

Reported because a job that has failed six times running is one somebody
needs to be shown rather than one that keeps quietly retrying.

action.description: What it does, or why it is reserved.

reaches_program.description: Whether the program underneath sees this key.

bindings.description: Every binding, in a stable order.
Every binding, and every reserved key.

Landed.description: One blob, as the list shows it.

refs.description: How many things are holding it open.

argv.description:
The argument vector, for an agent pane.

A vector, never a string. There is no shell in this path, so a prompt
containing a backtick is a prompt rather than an execution.

problems.description: Everything wrong with it, all at once.

panes.description:
The panes, in the order they should appear.

A flat list rather than a recursive split tree, and the reason is
worth stating: omt's own geometry tiles a flat list, so a tree would be
a shape the renderer immediately flattens. When the renderer grows
nested splits this grows with it, and not before — a schema that
describes something nothing can draw is a promise to nobody.

One entry per requested pane, in order.

Every pane, not just the failures: a layout that half-opened and said
"error" leaves somebody to work out which of six panes is missing.

hidden.description: Panes that survived but do not fit this screen.

missing.description:
Panes the layout named that are no longer running.

Named rather than counted, because a restore that quietly drops two
panes leaves somebody wondering what they have forgotten.

panes.description: The panes, in the order they should be arranged.

saved.description: How many layouts are saved now.

used.description: How many bytes are held in total.

can_rearrange.description: Whether this queue can be edited and reordered.

kind.description: `known` or `unknown`. Never an empty list standing in for `unknown`.

version.description: Its version, for a compare-and-swap edit.

Mapping.description: What omt can do with one directive.

oneOf.description: omt has something close, and the difference matters enough to ask.

name.description:
A name to prefer for the file, where the caller has one.

Advisory. The stem is taken from it and everything else is discarded:
the extension comes from what the bytes are, and a name is otherwise a
path traversal waiting to be written somewhere it was not meant to go.

path.description: The absolute path the bytes are now at.

digest.description: Its content digest, which is its identity in the blob store.

filename.description: A filename safe to write it as.

kind.description: What it is, judged from the bytes.

media_type.description: Its media type, where the bytes identify one.

calls.description: How many capability calls have been made.

failures.description: How many of those were refused.

marker.description: The contents of the store's version marker.

openable.description: Whether this build can open it.

steps.description: The migrations that would run, in order.

digest.description: A hash of what was fetched, so staleness is checkable.

read_only.description: Whether omt will refuse to write it back.

wrap.description: Whether to jump to the far side when there is nothing that way.

focus.description: Where focus should go, or nothing.

Offer.description: One thing that could be done.

label.description: What to call it in a menu.

mutates.description:
Whether it changes anything, so a confirm sheet is decidable without
running it.

commands.description: The slash commands, as the agent itself resolved them.

queue.description: The messages waiting to be sent.

OpenMatch.description: Something on a line that can be opened.

kind.description: What kind of thing it is.

line_number.description: The line number, for a path that carried one.

start.description: Where it starts in the line, in bytes.

OpenMatchOut.description: One match, as the preview shows it.

line_number.description: A line number, where the text carried one.

start.description: Byte offset of the first character.

matches.description: Everything found, in the order it appears.

Origin.description: Which tier a capability belongs to.

oneOf.description: Declared in the binary and checked by the macro.

Contributed by a plugin at run time, and validated by the host against
the same rules the macro applies — a plugin capability that fails them
is refused rather than registered in a degraded form.

version.description: Its version, so two installs of the same plugin are tellable apart.

closed.description: Whether there had been such a pane.

fit.description:
How many of them actually fit at the given size.

Reported so a client does not have to reimplement the rule: a pane too
small to use is worse than a pane that is not shown.

error.description: Why it did not, when it did not.

index.description: Its position in the request, so a caller can say *which* one.

focused.description: Whether it has focus — which is where typing goes.

session.description: The session it is looking at.

PaneTemplate.description: One pane in a launch configuration.

cwd.description: Where to run it, relative to the workspace. Absent means its root.

program.description: What to run. Absent means the user's shell.

PlacedIn.description: One placed pane, as the caller describes it.

placement_index.description: Its stable pre-order index, the total tie-break.

binary.description:
How to remove the binary, which omt will not do itself.

The binary is the package manager's business. A program that deletes
its own executable mid-run leaves a half-finished uninstall with
nothing left to finish it.

plan.description: A hash of this plan, which `uninstall.apply` must quote back.

steps.description: Every step, in the order it would run.

entry.description:
The program to run, with arguments. Empty for a plugin with nothing to
run — a theme or a keymap is a real plugin and must not be made to
invent an executable.

grant.description:
What is actually granted.

Separate from `permissions` on purpose: what a plugin asks for and what
it is allowed are different things, and collapsing them would make every
install a grant of everything requested.

refused.description:
What it asked for and did not get, so a UI can say so rather than
leaving the user to compare two lists.

socket.description: The socket to hand it. Absent means omt's default.

pid.description: The process id, so it can be found and stopped.

role.description:
The role its token carries — derived from what it was granted, never
from what it asked for.

high_consequence.description:
The grants that can do real damage, separated so a settings screen can
lead with them rather than bury them in a list of twelve.

index_reasoning.description: Whether the agent's reasoning is indexed.

indexed_tool_fields.description: Which fields of a tool call are indexed.

sources.description: Every source and what happens to it.

config.description:
The configuration text.

Passed in rather than read from `~/.tmux.conf`, so the web client can
preview a config the daemon's machine does not have — and so this can be
tested against a config that is not the tester's own.

mapped.description: How many omt can honour exactly.

preview.description: A hash of this preview, which apply must quote back.

review.description: How many need a decision before anything is written.

unsupported.description: How many omt cannot honour at all.

auth_backend.description: A password or bearer backend is configured.

bearer_device_bound.description: Bearer tokens are bound to a device key.

password_length.description: How long the configured password is.

rate_limited.description: Rate limiting and lockout are on.

tailnet_identity_only.description: The only identity available is the tailnet's.

origin.description:
Where they came from.

Taken from the caller because only the caller knows, and recorded rather
than acted on: what may be done with a blob depends on where it came
from, and that decision belongs at the point of use.

digest.description: Its content hash, which is its name.

kind.description: What it appears to be, sniffed rather than declared.

media_type.description: Its media type, where one could be determined.

freshness_secs.description: How long a verification counts for.

verified_secs_ago.description: How long since this device verified, in seconds. Absent means never.

because.description: Why it is asking, when it is.

failing_narrows_authority.description:
Whether failing narrows what the device may do.

Always false, and reported so a client cannot implement it as if it
might be true. A failed step-up is "not now", never "not you".

proceeds.description: Whether the call proceeds without a prompt.

exit_code.description: How it ended, where that is known.

held.description: How many commands are now held.

prefix.description: What has been typed so far.

workspace.description:
Which workspace is being typed in — suggestions are scored per
workspace, because the command you want in one repository is rarely the
command you want in another.

uses_here.description:
How often it has been run in this workspace, which is what a UI shows to
explain why the suggestion is there.

RefusalOut.description: Something that must be fixed first.

programs.description: How many programs omt knows the keymap of.

keys.description: One entry per key asked about.

pending.description:
Which of them will not take effect until something restarts.

Listed separately because that is the answer somebody needs. A setting
that quietly waits for a restart is the worst of the three: it is
changed, nothing happens, and the conclusion is that the setting does
not work.

ReloadEntry.description: One key and when a change to it takes effect.

path.description: The local path of the mirror to drop.

discarded.description: Whether anything was there to drop.

host.description: Which host, as ssh would name it.

decision.description: What omt would do about it.

uname.description: What the host said it is.

expected_text.description:
The text it is expected to still carry.

An id alone is a position, and a position in a draining queue is not a
stable target.

removed.description: Whether the entry is gone from omt's view.

topic.description: A topic name, or a capability name for the specific one.

RenderOut.description: What `help.render` reports: the overlay's model, not a rendered page.

expected_version.description: The ordering version this call was composed against.

order.description: Every entry id, in the order wanted.

what_happened.description: What the person was doing, in their words.

report.description:
The report, as text somebody can read before they send it.

Text rather than an opaque bundle, and returned rather than uploaded:
omt has no cloud to upload to, and a diagnostic somebody cannot read is
one they have to trust blindly about their own machine.

epoch.description: The writer epoch, checked like any other write.

command.description: What was sent, so a caller can show it rather than assuming.

line.description: A line, where the text carried one.

path.description: The path as it was recognised.

roots.description:
The roots it may resolve against.

Passed in rather than taken from the daemon's open workspaces, because
the caller knows which pane the text came from and the daemon does not.

actions.description: What can be done, best first.

existence.description: Whether it is there — or was not looked for.

line.description: A line, where there was one.

root.description: Which root it resolved against, so a wrong answer is visible.

agent_touched.description: Whether an agent was attributed to it.

compact_after_days.description: When it would be compacted, in days. Absent means never.

keep.description:
The device to keep, which is the one asking.

Required rather than optional. Revoking everything including the device
in your hand locks you out of the machine you were securing, and the
recovery for that is physical access — so there is no spelling of this
call that does it by accident.

Role.description:
How much authority a credential carries.

Roles answer *who you shared this instance with*. They are not a way to
degrade the owner's own devices: an authenticated `Operator` is equivalent
to sitting at the TUI, because access control decides who may connect, not
what they may do once connected.

oneOf.description: May do anything the owner can do at the terminal.
May also administer the instance itself.

files_disagreement.description: Files the two records disagree about.

tokens.description: Tokens, agent-reported. Absent means unreported, not zero.

rules.description: Every rule, in the order they are tried.

rule.description:
Which rule fired, if any.

Named rather than a bare boolean: "it matched" is not an answer
somebody can use to fix a rule that did not.

RunIn.description: One run, as the caller describes it.

base_ref.description: The resolved base it is measured against.

files_from_agent.description: Files the agent said it changed.

factors.description: Each factor, in the order applied.

from.description: Which absolute row the first one is.

total.description:
How many rows the session has ever written, so a client can size a
scrollbar without fetching everything behind it.

len.description: How long it is, in characters.

start.description: Where in the row the match starts, in characters.

text.description:
The whole line, so a result list can show context without a second call
per hit.

truncated.description:
Whether the limit cut the answer short, so a client can say "more"
rather than implying it found everything.

force.description: Take it even though somebody else holds it.

epoch.description: The epoch the caller now holds, which every write is checked against.

failed_only.description:
Only the ones that failed.

The filter a "jump to the last error" needs. 130 and 141 are not
failures — the first is Ctrl-C and the second is what `… | head` does to
everything upstream of it — so this is narrower than "non-zero".

shell_integration.description:
Whether this shell emits the marks at all.

False means no blocks will ever appear, which a UI should say rather
than showing an empty list that looks like "you have run nothing".

closed.description:
Whether it was there to close.

Closing something already gone is success, not an error: a client that
retried after a dropped acknowledgement must not be told it failed.

program.description: What to run. Absent means the user's shell.

workspace.description: Which workspace to start it in.

SessionId.description: One logical terminal: a PTY or a native agent connection, plus its state.

workspace.description: Only sessions in this workspace, where given.

history.description: How many lines of scrollback to include before the screen.

alternate_screen.description:
Whether a full-screen program is drawing.

A client rendering a transcript needs to know: while this is true the
program owns every cell and a line-oriented view of it is nonsense.

screen.description: The visible screen, one string per row.

released.description: Whether this caller had been holding it.

program.description: What to run. Absent means what it was running before.

kept_lines.description: How many lines of the old screen were kept above the separator.

session.description: The session, which keeps its id — anything referring to it still does.

alternate_screen.description: Whether a full-screen program is drawing.

cols.description: Columns, so a client can size itself without counting characters.

cursor.description: Where the cursor is, as (row, col).

cursor_visible.description: Whether the cursor should be drawn at all.

rows.description: One entry per row, each a list of runs.

SessionSummary.description: One session, as a client sees it.

agent.description:
Which agent is running in it, where one is.

The instance has always known this — a session's kind is fixed at
creation — and reported only the title. So every client that needed the
agent guessed from the title, and a guess is wrong for most of the
covered set: each agent has its own attachment syntax, and a reference
in the wrong one is silently ignored, which looks exactly like an agent
choosing not to read the file.

agent_state.description:
What that agent is doing, where omt can tell.

Separate from `state`, which is the *session's* lifecycle — running,
orphaned, exited. A session can be running while the agent in it is
waiting for a person, and those are the two facts a roster has to keep
apart.

blocked.description: How many of those are waiting for a human.

cwd.description: Its live working directory, which is not its workspace.

state.description: Where it is in its life.

threads.description:
How many agent threads are in it.

Here rather than left to a second call per session, because it is what
every surface reads to decide whether it is looking at an agent — which
screen a tap opens, and whether the conversation is offered at all. A
client that has to ask separately gets it wrong until it has asked.

epoch.description:
The writer-token epoch the caller believed it held.

Required, not optional. Input already in flight when the token changed
hands must be rejected rather than landing in somebody else's command
line, and a caller that could omit this would be a caller exempt from
the check.

bytes.description:
How many bytes went out.

Bytes written, not bytes delivered. The far side is a program omt does
not own, so a successful write proves the pipe accepted it and nothing
more.

SettingSchema.description: One thing a user can set.

choices.description: The permitted values, where there is a fixed set.

current.description: What it currently resolves to, and where that came from.

default.description: What it is when nobody has set it.

doc.description: One line about what it does.

layer.description: Which layer supplied the current value, absent when it is the default.

session.description:
Which session to judge by. Absent asks about the shell omt was started
from, which is what a fresh client with no session wants to know.

active.description:
Whether marks have actually been seen.

Observed rather than configured: a block with a command attributed to it
is proof that OSC 133 arrived. A setting could be wrong; this cannot.

blocks_seen.description:
How many blocks have been seen at all.

Reported so a caller can tell "no integration" from "nothing has
happened yet" — a brand-new session has seen nothing either way, and
telling somebody to install a snippet they already have is worse than
saying nothing.

shell.description: The shell, as far as omt can tell.

snippet.description:
The line to add, and where.

Absent when integration is already active, and absent for a shell omt
has no snippet for — returning bash's line for fish puts an error in
somebody's terminal on every login.

ShellSnippet.description: What to add to a shell's configuration.

force.description: Stop even if something is working.

blocked_by.description: What stopped it, when it is not.

SlashCommand.description: A slash command the agent itself resolved.

SourcePolicy.description: What omt does with one source.

bytes.description: The cap or window, in bytes, where there is one.

cost_usd.description:
Cost, **only** when the agent itself stated one.

Never computed. A price table in omt goes stale the week any provider
changes pricing, and the estimate would sit beside counts that are
right with nothing to tell them apart.

bootstrap.description: What to do if it did not.

remote_has_omt.description: Whether a probe found omt on the far side.

argv.description: The argument vector, with no shell involved.

direct_media.description: Whether paste crosses directly, or goes through the escape bridge.

mode.description: How the session would be run.

reason.description: Why, in words somebody can act on.

found.description: Whether there was a snapshot at all.

missing.description:
Roots the snapshot named that are no longer there.

Reported rather than dropped silently: a workspace that moved is
something the user can fix, and a restore that quietly opened four of
five looks like it worked.

sessions.description: How many sessions came back, orphaned.

path.description: Where to write it. Absent means omt's own state directory.

reason.description: Why, in words somebody can act on.

at_rest.description: What omt does and does not encrypt.

summary.description: One line somebody deciding whether to run this can read.

StyledRun.description:
A run of cells that share a style.

Runs rather than cells: a terminal screen is overwhelmingly long stretches
of one style, and a cell-per-element payload is roughly twenty times larger
for the same picture — which is the difference between a usable phone link
and an unusable one.

fg.description: Foreground, as `#rrggbb`, or absent for the theme's default.

inverse.description:
Inverse video, left for the client to apply so it can swap against
whatever its own default colours are.

state.description:
Where it is now.

`cancelling`, not `cancelled`: it stops at its next checkpoint, and
saying otherwise would have the caller believe it had already stopped.

outcome.description: What happened, once it is over.

include_finished.description: Include the ones that have finished.

cancellable.description: Whether it can still be stopped.

entry_resolved.description: Whether a terminfo entry for it could be resolved.

nested.description:
Whether omt is running inside another multiplexer.

Worth saying plainly: nested multiplexers are the single most common
reason a prefix key appears not to work, and somebody in that situation
has no way to tell from the screen.

program.description: What the outer terminal calls itself, where it says so.

ThemeOut.description: A theme as a client needs it.

ansi.description:
The sixteen ANSI colours in their conventional order, 0–15.

Sent as one flat list because that is the order every terminal and every
client indexes them by; splitting normal from bright would make every
consumer reassemble it.

appearance.description:
Whether it is meant for a light or a dark terminal.

Stated by the theme rather than guessed from the background, because a
borderline theme guessed wrong propagates into every contrast decision
a client then makes.

ThreadSummary.description: One thread — the session's own, or a subagent it spawned.

id.description: The agent's own id for it.

label.description: What it is working on, where it said.

open_interactions.description: Cards it raised that are still waiting.

omt_on_both_ends.description: omt answered on the far side of the connection.

osc_companion_answered.description: A companion on the near side acknowledged the OSC handshake.

reverse_socket_answered.description: A forwarded socket exists *and* an omt instance answered on it.

terminal_upload_confirmed.description: The terminal replied about its own upload protocol.

explanation.description: Why paste behaves the way it does, in words for a person.

count.description: How many identical events collapsed into it.

spanned_secs.description: From the first to the last, in seconds.

TimelineEventIn.description: One event, as the caller describes it.

at.description: When, in seconds since the epoch.

label.description: What it was, in the agent's own words.

digest.description: A short account for somebody who was away.

Topic.description: One topic: a capability group, and what is in it.

entries.description: The titles of what it holds, so a tree can be drawn without a second call.

name.description: The group name, which is the topic name.

from.description: Skip this many entries from the start.

dropped.description:
How many were dropped off the front of a long session, so a client says
the history is incomplete rather than presenting a partial one as whole.

total.description: How many the session holds in total.

UnmappedSetting.description: One setting omt could not map.

available.description: What is available, where omt could find out.

blocked_by.description: What is running that would be lost by restarting now.

delegate_to.description: The command to run instead, when a package manager owns the binary.

installed_by.description: How omt was installed, and therefore what should do the upgrading.

session.description: One session, or absent for the instance as a whole.

headroom.description:
`unknown` or `reported`.

`unknown` is the common case and must stay distinct from a low number:
a surface that drew silence as an empty bar would invent the one figure
a user acts on.

limit_status.description: What the agent said about its limit, when it said anything.

resets_at.description: When the agent said the limit resets.

session.description: This session's spend, when one was named.

sessions_reporting.description: How many sessions have reported anything at all.

oneOf.description: Looked, and it works but something is worth knowing.

Did not look. Never `ok`: an unrun check reported as passing is how a
diagnosis stops somebody investigating the thing that is actually wrong.

final_chunk.description:
Whether this is settled or still being revised.

The distinction is the whole design: a partial result is shown and then
replaced, and treating one as final puts a half-heard word into somebody's
command line permanently.

session.description: Which session is being dictated into.

committed.description: Only the settled part, which is what may be sent to a session.

display.description: Everything heard, settled and unsettled, for display.

had_text.description: Whether there had been anything to clear.

VoiceProvider.description: One speech engine this instance could use.

id.description: Its id, which is what configuration names.

key_present.description:
Whether a key is configured.

Presence, never the value. A capability that returned a key would put
it in a log the first time somebody debugged a client.

label.description: What to call it in a settings screen.

needs_key.description:
Whether it needs a credential at all — a local engine does not, and
demanding one would make the private option look like the hard one.

usable.description:
Whether dictation can currently do anything.

False on a fresh install, and that is the shipped state: no key, no
provider, and no audio leaving the machine until the user says where it
goes.

oneOf.description: The agent is waiting for a human to say something.
The agent needs a human before it can continue.
The agent is working on a turn.

A *new* interaction opened after the wait began.

An edge, not a state. A watcher that wants each card exactly once asks
for this; `Blocked` would fire immediately on a card it has already
handled.

immediate.description:
Resolve at once if the condition already holds.

Default true: the alternative is a guaranteed race, because a script
that checks and then waits misses the transition in between.

timeout_ms.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds.

until.description: Any of these ends the wait.

matched.description: Which condition ended it, if one did.

waited_ms.description: How long it waited, in milliseconds.

workspaces.description: Every workspace, in a stable order.

already_open.description:
Whether it was already open.

Reported rather than hidden: the id is derived from the path, so opening
twice is one workspace by construction, and a caller that expected to
create something should be able to see that it did not.

WorkspaceSummary.description: One workspace, as a client sees it.

root.description: Its canonical root, which is its identity.

branch.description: The branch to check out, created if it does not exist.

path.description:
Where to put it. Relative paths are resolved against the repository's
parent, so `../omt-feature` is the shape people actually use.

worktrees.description: Every worktree, the main checkout first.

force.description: Remove it even with uncommitted changes.

branch.description: The branch checked out in it, absent for a detached HEAD.

is_main.description:
Whether it is the repository's original checkout.

Reported because it cannot be removed, and a UI offering to is a UI
whose button fails.

path.description: Its absolute path, which is also what its workspace id derives from.

workspace.description:
The workspace id this path would open as.

Derived, not allocated: a worktree *is* a workspace the moment it
exists, and this saves a client computing the same hash.

capabilities.doc: Baselines are per binding and learned from its own history: thirty seconds is an eternity for a linter and a blink for a test suite, so a fixed threshold is wrong for everybody.
capabilities.name: agent.attention
capabilities.title: Is this agent stuck

capabilities.doc: Presents comparable facts; never ranks, scores or recommends. Judging requires understanding the code, and a plausible wrong recommendation about which branch to keep costs somebody real work.
capabilities.name: agent.compare
capabilities.title: Compare parallel runs

capabilities.doc: Run an agent's own protocol server and fold its notifications into the session's event stream. Anything the adapter cannot map is reported by name rather than dropped.
capabilities.name: agent.connect
capabilities.title: Connect a protocol agent

capabilities.doc: Stop an agent. For an agent with no protocol of its own this is the entire remote control surface.
capabilities.name: agent.interrupt
capabilities.title: Interrupt an agent

capabilities.doc: Slash commands, tools, models and the pending message queue, as the agent itself reported them. Never a list omt maintains: a completion popup offering a command the agent does not have is worse than none.
capabilities.name: agent.offers
capabilities.title: What an agent offers

capabilities.doc: Every thread in a session — the main one and each subagent — with what it is doing and any card it raised.
capabilities.name: agent.threads
capabilities.title: List agent threads

capabilities.doc: The primitive that stops every script being a sleep loop. `blocked` is a state and matches at once; `interaction` is an edge and matches only a card that opens after the wait began.
capabilities.name: agent.wait
capabilities.title: Wait for an agent

capabilities.doc: The screen and each named region of it. Rules written from memory are wrong in ways only a real screen finds: omt's own rule for Claude Code's permission prompt was written from memory and was wrong about the first screen anybody sees.
capabilities.name: agent_rules.capture
capabilities.title: Capture a screen for writing rules

capabilities.doc: Which rule won, where it looked, and what it concluded. A wrong answer that cannot be traced to a rule is one people argue about.
capabilities.name: agent_rules.explain
capabilities.title: Explain a screen verdict

capabilities.doc: Only when asked, and only after the checks. omt never fetches, updates or applies a rule set on a timer or at startup: a matcher that runs against somebody's screen arrives because they decided, or not at all.
capabilities.name: agent_rules.import
capabilities.title: Install a rule set

capabilities.doc: What it would change, before anything changes. A rule set is a matcher that runs against whatever is on the screen, so installing one is an act rather than an update.
capabilities.name: agent_rules.inspect
capabilities.title: Inspect a rule set

capabilities.doc: Every call, with who made it and whether it worked. Refusals included: a log of only what succeeded answers the wrong question, because who *tried* to do what is most of what an audit is for.
capabilities.name: audit.list
capabilities.title: What has been done

capabilities.doc: The output of one command block, as styled lines. Paged, because a block can hold a whole test run and a phone asking for one over a slow link stalls.
capabilities.name: block.body
capabilities.title: Read a block's output

capabilities.doc: Send a block's command to its session again. Refused for a block omt never saw the command of, because the alternative is scraping the screen for something that looks like a prompt.
capabilities.name: block.rerun
capabilities.title: Re-run a command

capabilities.doc: Resolved settings, each with the layer and file it came from — which is what makes a surprising value traceable.
capabilities.name: config.get
capabilities.title: Read configuration

capabilities.doc: Translate another terminal's settings into omt's, reporting what did not map rather than dropping it. A query: it says what the import would be, and writing it is a separate decision somebody makes.
capabilities.name: config.import
capabilities.title: Import settings

capabilities.doc: A setting that quietly waits for a restart is changed, nothing happens, and the conclusion is that the setting does not work.
capabilities.name: config.reload_class
capabilities.title: When a setting takes effect

capabilities.doc: Every setting with its default, type and description — so a settings screen can be built without knowing the key names in advance. `config.get` reports what is set; this reports what could be.
capabilities.name: config.schema
capabilities.title: List every setting

capabilities.doc: Every device that has been let in, by the name it gave. Pairing mints a credential per device, and a credential nobody can see is one nobody revokes.
capabilities.name: device.list
capabilities.title: List paired devices

capabilities.doc: The label is the only thing distinguishing two devices in a list, and a list of three `iPhone`s is one nobody can revoke from — so renaming is part of revocation working.
capabilities.name: device.rename
capabilities.title: Rename a device

capabilities.doc: Stop one device's credential working, leaving every other device alone. This is what makes a lost phone something somebody can act on.
capabilities.name: device.revoke
capabilities.title: Revoke a device

capabilities.doc: The `I lost a device and do not know which` button. Keeps the one asking, because revoking that too locks somebody out of the machine they were securing.
capabilities.name: device.revoke_all
capabilities.title: Revoke every other device

capabilities.doc: The diagnosis, the version and what the person was doing, as readable text they can check before sending. Nothing is uploaded: omt has no cloud, and a report somebody cannot read is one they have to trust blindly about their own machine.
capabilities.name: doctor.report
capabilities.title: Write a bug report

capabilities.doc: Per-link diagnosis with a remedy on every failure. A check this build cannot perform is reported as not checked rather than as passing: an unrun check reported green is how a diagnosis stops somebody investigating the real problem.
capabilities.name: doctor.run
capabilities.title: Diagnose this instance

capabilities.doc: Subscribe to the event stream.
capabilities.name: events.subscribe
capabilities.title: Subscribe to events

capabilities.doc: Record which arm won, naming its branch. Merges nothing and deletes nothing: the losing worktrees are what you would look at to check the choice was right.
capabilities.name: fanout.choose
capabilities.title: Choose an arm

capabilities.doc: Create a worktree per agent and record them as one fan-out. Every arm is reported, including any that could not be prepared.
capabilities.name: fanout.start
capabilities.title: Fan a prompt across agents

capabilities.doc: Every arm of every fan-out, with its worktree, branch and state.
capabilities.name: fanout.status
capabilities.title: Fan-out status

capabilities.doc: List a directory inside a workspace. Paths are workspace-relative and cannot escape it.
capabilities.name: fs.list
capabilities.title: List files

capabilities.doc: Read one chunk of a file. Chunked so a large file over a slow link can show progress and resume rather than restarting.
capabilities.name: fs.read
capabilities.title: Read a file

capabilities.doc: Write one chunk of a file into a workspace. The file appears only once every chunk has arrived.
capabilities.name: fs.write
capabilities.title: Write a file

capabilities.doc: Which files changed, with line counts. Staged and unstaged are separate answers.
capabilities.name: git.diff
capabilities.title: Git diff

capabilities.doc: The changed lines of one file. `git.diff` reports which files changed; this is what changed in them. Returned as lines rather than rendered, because a terminal, a phone and a browser each want to draw it differently.
capabilities.name: git.hunks
capabilities.title: Diff a file

capabilities.doc: Branch, divergence and working-tree state. Reads only — nothing here commits, checks out or fetches.
capabilities.name: git.status
capabilities.title: Git status

capabilities.doc: A model rather than formatted text, so a phone and a terminal can render the same help differently without one of them parsing the other's layout.
capabilities.name: help.render
capabilities.title: Show help for a topic

capabilities.doc: Derived from the catalog, not written beside it. Hand-written help is wrong the first time something is renamed and stays wrong, because nothing fails when it drifts.
capabilities.name: help.topics
capabilities.title: Browse help

capabilities.doc: The targeted counterpart to a store purge: somebody who typed a secret into a shell wants that line gone, not their whole history. Every run of a matching command goes, not only the most recent.
capabilities.name: history.forget
capabilities.title: Forget commands

capabilities.doc: The instance-scoped query and the only implementation; `scope` narrows it. History exists where blocks exist, so a shell with no integration contributes nothing rather than guesses.
capabilities.name: history.query
capabilities.title: Search command history

capabilities.doc: Every person this instance knows and the devices each holds. A credential answers whether a token may do something; this answers whose phone it is, which is what makes revoking somebody's access — rather than one token — expressible.
capabilities.name: identity.list
capabilities.title: Who holds what

capabilities.doc: A proof-of-presence timer, not an authorisation narrowing. Failing it means the device must show a human is holding it, and then it may do everything again.
capabilities.name: identity.reauth_check
capabilities.title: Does this need a fresh check

capabilities.doc: Revoke every device one person holds, in one action. Doing it device by device means somebody who has left keeps whichever one was missed, and there is no moment at which their access is known to be gone.
capabilities.name: identity.revoke
capabilities.title: Revoke a person's access

capabilities.doc: Every capability this instance offers.
capabilities.name: instance.catalog
capabilities.title: List capabilities

capabilities.doc: Version and protocol of this instance.
capabilities.name: instance.info
capabilities.title: Instance info

capabilities.doc: Clients, sessions, calls and refusals. The health route says the process is up and says nothing else, which is not the same as knowing it is doing anything.
capabilities.name: instance.metrics
capabilities.title: How the instance is doing

capabilities.doc: Refuses while an agent is working or blocked, naming the sessions. A shutdown that takes an agent down mid-turn is the same loss an upgrade refuses to cause.
capabilities.name: instance.shutdown
capabilities.title: Shut down

capabilities.doc: Every interaction waiting for a human, with whether omt can answer it from here and why not when it cannot.
capabilities.name: interaction.list
capabilities.title: List open questions

capabilities.doc: Answer an open interaction. Exactly once: a second answer is refused with who won, and answerability comes from the deliverable rather than the state.
capabilities.name: interaction.resolve
capabilities.title: Answer a question

capabilities.doc: A fresh invite, so a second device can be paired from a device already paired. Without it the only invite is the one printed at startup, and adding a phone means restarting the instance everybody else is connected to.
capabilities.name: invite.create
capabilities.title: Invite another device

capabilities.doc: Create a scheduled job, replacing any job of the same name. A missed window is skipped rather than caught up.
capabilities.name: job.create
capabilities.title: Schedule a job

capabilities.doc: Scheduled jobs with when they fire and how many times each has failed in a row.
capabilities.name: job.list
capabilities.title: List scheduled jobs

capabilities.doc: A registry nobody runs the defaults against documents a problem instead of preventing one.
capabilities.name: keys.audit
capabilities.title: Audit omt's own bindings

capabilities.doc: Every binding and every reserved key, generated from the keymap in force so it cannot go stale.
capabilities.name: keys.cheatsheet
capabilities.title: Keyboard reference

capabilities.doc: A binding naming a capability that is not there parses, loads and does nothing — and the person who wrote it concludes their key is broken rather than their spelling.
capabilities.name: keys.check_file
capabilities.title: Check a keybinding file

capabilities.doc: `Conflicts with something` is not actionable — every chord collides somewhere. This says which program, what the key does there, and how badly it would be missed.
capabilities.name: keys.conflicts
capabilities.title: What a binding would break

capabilities.doc: `Not bound` and `bound, but the pane underneath owns it` look identical from the user's chair and have different fixes, so this says which.
capabilities.name: keys.explain
capabilities.title: Explain a key

capabilities.doc: A modal keymap governs omt's own surfaces only. It never governs a pane whose keys are passing through, which is what stops omt and an inner vim from contending over hjkl.
capabilities.name: keys.flavour
capabilities.title: vim or emacs bindings

capabilities.doc: In a stable order, so two calls can be compared. An unordered list makes a diff between two configurations unreadable.
capabilities.name: keys.list
capabilities.title: List every binding

capabilities.doc: The registry is data, so a new agent CLI is a file rather than a release. This says how much of it is loaded.
capabilities.name: keys.registry
capabilities.title: Known inner keymaps

capabilities.doc: An agent is spawned with an argument vector, never by typing into a shell — a launch file is copied from a colleague and the prompt is the part people edit.
capabilities.name: launch.preview
capabilities.title: Preview a launch configuration

capabilities.doc: Start several sessions as a layout, reporting the outcome of every pane rather than only that something failed.
capabilities.name: layout.open
capabilities.title: Open a layout

capabilities.doc: Keeps the panes that still exist and names the rest. Failing outright gives somebody nothing; keeping dead names gives them panes they have to close one by one.
capabilities.name: layout.restore
capabilities.title: Restore a saved layout

capabilities.doc: The tree and nothing else. Rects are a function of the tree and the screen, so saving them would restore a desktop layout onto a phone as a desktop layout.
capabilities.name: layout.save
capabilities.title: Save this layout

capabilities.doc: Per-adapter, because one format applied to all of them is silently ignored by most — which looks exactly like an agent choosing not to read the file.
capabilities.name: media.attach
capabilities.title: Reference a file to an agent

capabilities.doc: OSC 52, wrapped for tmux when TERM says so. omt does not claim the copy succeeded: there is no acknowledgement to base that on.
capabilities.name: media.clipboard
capabilities.title: Copy to local clipboard

capabilities.doc: What a blob is, from its bytes rather than from a filename somebody supplied. A name is a claim; the bytes are the evidence, and writing an executable as a `.png` is what trusting the claim allows.
capabilities.name: media.describe
capabilities.title: Identify a blob

capabilities.doc: By digest, which is the only name a blob has. There is no path to traverse because there is no path.
capabilities.name: media.get
capabilities.title: Fetch a blob

capabilities.doc: A landing zone nobody can see the contents of is one that has quietly become the place things live.
capabilities.name: media.list
capabilities.title: List blobs

capabilities.doc: Under omt's managed root, never inside the workspace: an attachment written into the repository is an unreviewed file from a phone sitting in somebody's working tree.
capabilities.name: media.materialize
capabilities.title: Write a blob to a path

capabilities.doc: A tier is never claimed without a positive handshake. `Probably` means a paste that silently does nothing, and no way for the user to tell whether they mis-copied or omt mis-guessed.
capabilities.name: media.paste_tier
capabilities.title: How paste reaches this machine

capabilities.doc: The type is sniffed here and never taken from the sender. A sender that names its own content type decides how the receiver treats it.
capabilities.name: media.put
capabilities.title: Upload a blob

capabilities.doc: Every directive comes back classified, including the ones omt cannot map. A migration that silently drops a third of somebody's bindings fails without ever reporting an error.
capabilities.name: migrate.tmux_preview
capabilities.title: Preview a tmux config

capabilities.doc: Every trigger is something the user produced, and every feature is mentioned at most once. Advocacy for a feature somebody has not yet needed spends attention omt will want later.
capabilities.name: onboarding.disclosures
capabilities.title: Advanced features

capabilities.doc: Permanent. Somebody who turns tips off and is asked again next week has been told their answer did not count.
capabilities.name: onboarding.dismiss_hints
capabilities.title: Stop showing tips

capabilities.doc: At most one hint is ever offered. Six tips on a first run teach nobody six things; they teach that omt interrupts.
capabilities.name: onboarding.hint_state
capabilities.title: Show the next tip

capabilities.doc: When the program in the pane has mouse reporting on, every press is its input. A multiplexer that swallows clicks so its own link handler can run has broken vim, and no link feature is worth that.
capabilities.name: open.click
capabilities.title: Who owns this click

capabilities.doc: Paths, URLs and file:line references on a line of output, with their offsets — so a client can make them tappable without inventing its own pattern.
capabilities.name: open.recognize
capabilities.title: Find links and paths

capabilities.doc: Unpins the blob so the sweeper can take it. Discarding something already gone is reported, not an error — a retry after a lost acknowledgement must not look like a failure.
capabilities.name: open.remote_discard
capabilities.title: Discard a mirrored file

capabilities.doc: A mirror nobody can see is a copy of somebody's file sitting on disk with no way to tell where it came from or to get rid of it.
capabilities.name: open.remote_list
capabilities.title: List mirrored remote files

capabilities.doc: A path resolved against the wrong root opens somebody else's file, so the root that was used is part of the answer and anything escaping every root is refused rather than clamped.
capabilities.name: open.resolve
capabilities.title: Resolve a recognised path

capabilities.doc: A recognition system nobody can enumerate is one where `why did that not become a link` has no answer short of reading the source.
capabilities.name: open.rules_list
capabilities.title: List recognition rules

capabilities.doc: Powers the config editor's live preview. Names the rule that fired, because a preview that only says whether something matched cannot help fix one that did not.
capabilities.name: open.rules_test
capabilities.title: Test a line against the rules

capabilities.doc: Close a pane. The session it showed keeps running — closing a view of something is not ending it.
capabilities.name: pane.close
capabilities.title: Close a pane

capabilities.doc: Move focus to a pane, which is where typing goes. Focusing a pane that is not there is refused rather than silently ignored.
capabilities.name: pane.focus
capabilities.title: Focus a pane

capabilities.doc: Panes in a workspace's primary view, which one has focus, and how many fit on a standard terminal.
capabilities.name: pane.list
capabilities.title: List panes

capabilities.doc: Geometric, over the placed rectangles rather than tree order — tree order gives wrong answers in asymmetric layouts. Deterministic, because breaking ties by recency makes the same keypress do two different things for reasons the user cannot see.
capabilities.name: pane.navigate
capabilities.title: Move focus in a direction

capabilities.doc: Open a pane onto an existing session. Presentation only: no process is started and none is stopped.
capabilities.name: pane.open
capabilities.title: Open a pane

capabilities.doc: Switch a plugin on or off. Idempotent: setting the state it already has is not an error.
capabilities.name: plugin.enable
capabilities.title: Enable a plugin

capabilities.doc: Install a plugin with an explicit grant. What it asks for and what it receives are separate, and what was refused is reported.
capabilities.name: plugin.install
capabilities.title: Install a plugin

capabilities.doc: Installed plugins with what each was granted, and which of those grants are high-consequence.
capabilities.name: plugin.list
capabilities.title: List plugins

capabilities.doc: Run a plugin, handing it a socket and a token whose role comes from what it was granted. A plugin reaches omt through the same capability surface as any other client — there is no second API.
capabilities.name: plugin.start
capabilities.title: Start a plugin

capabilities.doc: Every client connected right now. "Is somebody else looking at this" is a question people ask before they type, and a terminal that cannot answer it is one where two people interleave keystrokes into one shell.
capabilities.name: presence.list
capabilities.title: Who is connected

capabilities.doc: Unsupported on an agent's own queue, which emits enqueue and remove and no third verb. The pair is not a substitute: the removal is the unconfirmable half.
capabilities.name: queue.edit
capabilities.title: Edit a queued message

capabilities.doc: Takes a binding rather than a session. A replayed enqueue against a session whose agent has exited types the text into a shell prompt, where it runs as a command.
capabilities.name: queue.enqueue
capabilities.title: Queue a message

capabilities.doc: Reports `unknown` when the reader is stale or has never spoken. An empty queue is a claim, and a broken reader must not be able to make it.
capabilities.name: queue.list
capabilities.title: List the queue

capabilities.doc: Never retried automatically: a repeated removal against a queue that has since drained removes a different message.
capabilities.name: queue.remove
capabilities.title: Remove a queued message

capabilities.doc: This is what a client's queue-reorder check asks for. Unsupported on an agent's own queue, and the client hides the drag handles rather than disabling them.
capabilities.name: queue.reorder
capabilities.title: Reorder the queue

capabilities.doc: A search index nobody can enumerate is one nobody can reason about. Reasoning is excluded by default: it is the most privacy-sensitive text an agent produces.
capabilities.name: recall.policy
capabilities.title: What is indexed

capabilities.doc: Add a command to the history that suggestions are drawn from.
capabilities.name: recall.record
capabilities.title: Record a command

capabilities.doc: Commands from history matching a prefix, scored by use in this workspace. Destructive commands are never suggested.
capabilities.name: recall.suggest
capabilities.title: Suggest a command

capabilities.doc: Operator, not Viewer, because it makes this machine reach out to a host the caller chose. Viewer with NETWORK has no carve-out.
capabilities.name: remote.probe
capabilities.title: Probe a host

capabilities.doc: A transparent weighted product with no learning and no hidden state. Search over somebody's own history is where a wrong answer looks exactly like a right one, and a ranker that cannot explain itself gives them no way to notice.
capabilities.name: search.explain
capabilities.title: Why this result ranked here

capabilities.doc: Find text across a session's screen and history, with the row and offsets of each hit so a client can scroll to it and highlight exactly that span.
capabilities.name: search.session
capabilities.title: Search a session

capabilities.doc: A misconfiguration fails the daemon rather than warning. A warning about an open port is printed once, into a log nobody reads, on a machine that is now reachable from the network.
capabilities.name: security.bind_check
capabilities.title: Check a listen configuration

capabilities.doc: Funnel puts the instance on the open internet, and the difference between that and a tailnet is not visible in any configuration omt reads. Somebody who enabled it for a demo and forgot is who this is for.
capabilities.name: security.publish_check
capabilities.title: Check before publishing

capabilities.doc: Take the writer token for a session, returning the epoch every write is checked against.
capabilities.name: session.acquire
capabilities.title: Take the writer token

capabilities.doc: Commands run in a session with their output ranges and exit codes, from OSC 133. A shell that emits no marks reports none rather than guesses.
capabilities.name: session.blocks
capabilities.title: List command blocks

capabilities.doc: The thing every migrating script asks for first. Reports the total as well as what it returned, so a truncated capture is visible rather than looking complete.
capabilities.name: session.capture
capabilities.title: Capture scrollback

capabilities.doc: End a session and stop the process on it. Idempotent.
capabilities.name: session.close
capabilities.title: Close a session

capabilities.doc: Start a session in a workspace, running a program on a pty. Deduplicated by intent id, so a reconnect retry does not start a second process.
capabilities.name: session.create
capabilities.title: Start a session

capabilities.doc: Every session this instance holds, optionally filtered to one workspace.
capabilities.name: session.list
capabilities.title: List sessions

capabilities.doc: The visible screen as text, optionally with scrollback.
capabilities.name: session.read
capabilities.title: Read a session

capabilities.doc: Give up the writer token. Idempotent: releasing one you do not hold is not an error.
capabilities.name: session.release
capabilities.title: Give up the writer token

capabilities.doc: Resize a session. The grid and the kernel are told together, so a program is never handed a size the kernel disagrees with.
capabilities.name: session.resize
capabilities.title: Resize a session

capabilities.doc: Respawn the command behind a session restored from a snapshot, keeping the old output above a separator.
capabilities.name: session.restart
capabilities.title: Restart a session

capabilities.doc: History as styled lines, by absolute row. Structured rather than raw bytes, so a browser needs no second terminal emulator to show what scrolled past.
capabilities.name: session.scrollback
capabilities.title: Read scrollback

capabilities.doc: The visible screen as styled runs, so a remote client renders the same picture as the terminal without emulating one.
capabilities.name: session.snapshot
capabilities.title: Snapshot a session

capabilities.doc: Derived from the event log, so it can be rebuilt at any time. Only consecutive identical calls collapse, and the canonicaliser strips whitespace and nothing else — one that ignored arguments would collapse `rm -rf build` and `rm -rf /`.
capabilities.name: session.timeline
capabilities.title: What happened here

capabilities.doc: Messages, reasoning, tool calls and results for an agent session. An agent emits no command marks, so blocks do not apply to it; this is what it is read through instead.
capabilities.name: session.transcript
capabilities.title: Read an agent transcript

capabilities.doc: Write input to a session, gated on the writer token's epoch.
capabilities.name: session.write
capabilities.title: Type into a session

capabilities.doc: Every agent omt can drive, found or not. Listing only what is present hides the difference between an agent omt did not find and one it has never heard of.
capabilities.name: setup.detect_agents
capabilities.title: Find installed agents

capabilities.doc: Whether the shell emits command marks, judged by what has been seen rather than by a setting, with the line that enables them. omt prints it and never edits a shell's configuration itself.
capabilities.name: shell.integration
capabilities.title: Shell integration status

capabilities.doc: An argument vector, never a shell string: a hostname from a config file with a quote in it would otherwise become remote execution.
capabilities.name: ssh.plan
capabilities.title: Preview an omt ssh session

capabilities.doc: Reopen the workspaces from a snapshot, reporting any whose directory is gone rather than dropping them silently.
capabilities.name: state.restore
capabilities.title: Restore instance state

capabilities.doc: Write the open workspaces to a snapshot a later run can restore. Written atomically: a crash mid-write leaves the previous snapshot, never half of a new one.
capabilities.name: state.save
capabilities.title: Save instance state

capabilities.doc: There is no best-effort partial parse. A partial read of a newer format silently drops whatever that version added, and writes the store back without it.
capabilities.name: store.migrate_status
capabilities.title: Can this store be opened

capabilities.doc: The alternative to this list is finding out what omt persists by reading twelve crates, which nobody does — least of all somebody deciding whether to run it on a work machine.
capabilities.name: store.paths
capabilities.title: What omt writes down

capabilities.doc: So somebody can find out what the detector catches before trusting it with something, rather than after.
capabilities.name: store.redaction_test
capabilities.title: Try the redactor

capabilities.doc: Compact first, delete second. The output of a build from three months ago is worthless; the fact that you ran it, where, and that it failed, is still useful and costs two hundred bytes.
capabilities.name: store.retention
capabilities.title: What happens to this data

capabilities.doc: Cooperative: it stops at its next checkpoint. One past its point of no return refuses with the reason rather than reporting a success it cannot deliver.
capabilities.name: task.cancel
capabilities.title: Cancel an operation

capabilities.doc: Where one operation got to, so a client that reconnected mid-job learns the answer it can no longer hear.
capabilities.name: task.get
capabilities.title: Get a running operation

capabilities.doc: 22 §10.1's job registry. Named `task` because `job` already means a scheduled job, and one name for two things would resolve by load order.
capabilities.name: task.list
capabilities.title: List running operations

capabilities.doc: A wrong TERM does not fail; it draws a subtly wrong screen that people blame on omt for weeks. This says what is advertised, what was observed, and where they disagree.
capabilities.name: term.profile
capabilities.title: Check this terminal

capabilities.doc: The colours in force, so a remote client renders a session in the user's own theme rather than in its own defaults.
capabilities.name: theme.get
capabilities.title: Read the theme

capabilities.doc: Refuses unless it is given the hash of a plan that still matches the disk. A confirmation against a plan that has since changed is a confirmation of something the user never saw.
capabilities.name: uninstall.apply
capabilities.title: Uninstall omt

capabilities.doc: Driven by the setup manifest. Anything absent from it is never touched — an uninstall that reasons about what it probably wrote eventually removes somebody else's configuration.
capabilities.name: uninstall.plan
capabilities.title: Preview an uninstall

capabilities.doc: omt never checks on its own. This reaches the network because the user typed it, and reports who owns the binary so a package manager's file is delegated to rather than overwritten.
capabilities.name: upgrade.check
capabilities.title: Check for an upgrade

capabilities.doc: Tokens spent per session and in total, with whatever the agent said about its rate limit. Cost appears only when the agent stated one — omt never computes it from a price table of its own.
capabilities.name: usage.report
capabilities.title: Usage and quota

capabilities.doc: Append a transcript chunk to a session's dictation buffer. Partial chunks are replaced by later ones; only the settled part is offered for sending.
capabilities.name: voice.append
capabilities.title: Add dictated text

capabilities.doc: Discard a session's dictation buffer. Idempotent.
capabilities.name: voice.clear
capabilities.title: Clear dictation

capabilities.doc: Speech-to-text engines this instance can use, and whether each has a key. Presence only — a capability that returned a key would put it in the first log somebody captured.
capabilities.name: voice.providers
capabilities.title: List speech engines

capabilities.doc: Every workspace this instance has open, with its session count.
capabilities.name: workspace.list
capabilities.title: List workspaces

capabilities.doc: Open a workspace at a canonical path. Idempotent: the id is derived from the path.
capabilities.name: workspace.open
capabilities.title: Open a workspace

capabilities.doc: Create a git worktree, which becomes a workspace by the id its path derives. Additive: it touches nothing that already exists, and a path already in use is refused rather than overwritten.
capabilities.name: worktree.add
capabilities.title: Add a worktree

capabilities.doc: Every worktree of a workspace's repository, with the workspace id each would open as. Read from git rather than from omt's own records, so it cannot disagree with reality.
capabilities.name: worktree.list
capabilities.title: List worktrees

capabilities.doc: Remove a worktree. Refused when it has uncommitted changes unless force is given — an agent's output is usually why the worktree was wanted, and deleting it on a tap is unrecoverable.
capabilities.name: worktree.remove
capabilities.title: Remove a worktree
